Jangling
JANG-gling
noun
From the Old French jangler, “to chatter, to quarrel, to gossip”; hence wrangling, discordant talk — the word carries the sound of a bell struck out of tune, noise where music should be.

Biblical Definition

Jangling is wrangling — discordant, quarrelsome talk, the noise of men disputing to no end. The word itself sounds like a bell struck badly, and that is the point: where the doctrine of God should ring clear, there is only clatter. Paul charges Timothy against it at the outset: the end of the commandment is charity out of a pure heart, and a good conscience, and faith unfeigned, “from which some having swerved have turned aside unto vain jangling” (1Ti 1:6). Mark the order — they did not begin as janglers; they swerved. Men leave the aim of love and a clean conscience, and having lost the mark they must do something with their religion, so they wrangle. Paul names them exactly: “Desiring to be teachers of the law; understanding neither what they say, nor whereof they affirm” (1Ti 1:7). The jangler is confident and ignorant at once, ambitious to teach and unable to explain. The charge is repeated at the end of the epistle: “keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called” (1Ti 6:20), and again to Timothy’s successor-charge, “charging them before the Lord that they strive not about words to no profit, but to the subverting of the hearers” (2Ti 2:14). Word-striving is never neutral. It profits nothing and it subverts the hearers — it pulls down the very people it was supposed to instruct. The remedy is not silence but the trust: keep the deposit, preach the commandment, and let the jangling alone.

Webster 1828 Definition

Wrangling; quarrelsome, discordant talk; disputing about words to no profit.

JANGLE, to quarrel in words; to wrangle; to sound discordantly, as an untuned bell.

From the Old French jangler, “to chatter, to quarrel.”

Vain jangling is the empty word-strife of those who have swerved from charity (1Ti 1:6).

The jangler desires to be a teacher of the law and understands neither what he says nor whereof he affirms (1Ti 1:7).

Striving about words profits nothing and subverts the hearers (2Ti 2:14).

Key Scripture

1Ti 1:6 — "From which some having swerved have turned aside unto vain jangling;"

1Ti 1:7 — "Desiring to be teachers of the law; understanding neither what they say, nor whereof they affirm."

1Ti 6:20 — "O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called:"

2Ti 2:14 — "Of these things put them in remembrance, charging them before the Lord that they strive not about words to no profit, but to the subverting of the hearers."

Modern Corruption

A live corruption: the endless online religious quarrel is vain jangling with a larger congregation — confident, ignorant, and subverting the hearers.

expand to see more

The corruption is not in the word, which needs no defending, but in a practice our age has industrialized. Vain jangling now runs continuously: the professing Christian whose whole religion is the argument, who desires to be a teacher of the law and understands neither what he says nor whereof he affirms, who has an opinion on every controversy and charity out of a pure heart on none. Paul’s diagnosis is precise and unflattering — such men swerved. They left the end of the commandment, which is love from a clean conscience and faith unfeigned, and having abandoned the aim they kept the vocabulary, and the vocabulary went sour into noise. A bell out of tune still rings; that is the trouble.

The apostle will not let this pass as a harmless pastime. Striving about words is “to no profit, but to the subverting of the hearers” — it does not merely fail to build, it pulls down; the onlookers are the casualties. And the janglers are always sure of themselves; confidence and ignorance keep close company. The remedy Paul gives is not a vow of silence but a deposit to guard: “keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called.” A man with a trust to keep has no time to jangle. Contend earnestly for the faith once delivered — that is commanded; wrangle about words for the pleasure of wrangling — that is forbidden, and the difference is the pure heart.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means wrangling, quarrelsome and discordant talk, disputing to no profit.

expand to see more

Jangle — Old French jangler, “to chatter, to quarrel, to gossip.”

It carries the sound of a bell struck out of tune — noise where music should be.

Vain jangling is what men turn aside to when they swerve from charity (1Ti 1:6).

The jangler would teach the law and understands neither what he says nor whereof he affirms.

Word-strife profits nothing and subverts the hearers (2Ti 2:14).

Usage

"Some having swerved have turned aside unto vain jangling — the noise begins where the aim was lost."

"The jangler desires to teach the law and understands neither what he says nor whereof he affirms."

"Keep that which is committed to thy trust: a man with a deposit to guard has no time to jangle."
